tagline.text: Fifteen minutes by boat from Davao, a garden island right next door

location.label: Location
location.text: Island Garden City of Samal, Davao del Norte

image.credit: Lachlan Fearnley / CC BY-SA 3.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: An island just
10–15 minutes

by boat from downtown Davao, officially named "Island Garden City of Samal." With white sand beach resorts, the world's largest known colony of fruit bats, and a sandbar that vanishes at high tide, it's a beloved getaway for Davao travelers.
Samal Island sits in the middle of Davao Gulf, separated from downtown Davao by a strait only about
1–2 km
wide. The whole island forms a single city, officially named "Island Garden City of Samal (IGACOS)." At about
300 km
², it's larger than it looks, with white sand, mangroves, and coral reefs alternating around the coastline. Nearby Talikud Island also belongs to Samal City and can be explored on the same trip.

Samal's biggest advantage is how accessible it is. Landing at Davao Airport and lying on a beach resort's lounge chair within an hour is a rare combination in the Philippines. That makes it a weekend family getaway for Davao locals, and for travelers, a place to combine city sightseeing with beach relaxation in one trip. Davao Gulf is sheltered by islands and peninsulas, keeping the waves gentle, and it lies outside the Philippines' main typhoon path, so swimming is possible year-round.

The island ranges from budget public beaches to upscale resorts with their own private docks. Pearl Farm Beach Resort, built on the site of a former pearl farm, is regarded as one of the Philippines' leading luxury resorts. In the northern Babak area, the Monfort Bat Sanctuary is home to an estimated 1.8 million Geoffroy's rousette fruit bats, recognized by Guinness World Records as the world's largest colony of fruit bats.
Construction is now under way on the Samal–Davao Connector Bridge, about
long, linking Davao City to Samal Island. As of
, construction is more than 60% complete, targeting completion in
— once finished, you'll be able to reach the island by car in about
5 minutes
instead of by boat. For now, it's still a chance to enjoy the leisurely pace of an island trip by boat. It suits family travelers, couples, and business travelers or residents based in Davao.

A cave on a private farm in the Babak area, where you can look up from below at bats packed densely into every crevice at the cave entrance. At dusk, you may catch the spectacle of huge numbers of bats taking flight in search of food.

Even without staying overnight, you can pay for a day pass to use a resort's beach and pool for the day. Options range from budget public beaches to upscale resorts with meal credits included, to suit any budget.
A sandbar off the island's southwest coast that appears only at low tide and disappears under the sea at high tide. You can take a bangka out to walk the exposed sandbar and snorkel nearby.
A tiered waterfall in the forest of the Peñaplata area inland, with several small falls and pools for swimming. It offers a cool freshwater swim as a change from the sea.

blocks.title: Snorkeling and diving at Talikud Island

children.text: A small island south of Samal, where the surrounding coral gardens and marine protected areas are good for snorkeling and diving. It's quieter and clearer than Samal, making it a good day trip.
A wide public beach in Kaputian in the island's south, popular with local families for its fine sand and cheap cottage rentals. It's a good place to see everyday Filipino beach culture up close.

A route around the coastal road by chartered habal-habal or multicab, stopping at beaches, villages, and viewpoints. On the island's east coast, you can see the mountains across Davao Gulf and the sunrise.

Charter a multicab or habal-habal and visit the Monfort Bat Sanctuary first.
Enjoy a freshwater swim at Hagimit Falls.
Enjoy lunch, swimming, and rest at a beach resort with a day pass.
Head back to the wharf and take the boat back to Davao. The Davao skyline at dusk from the boat is beautiful.
Cross to the island in the morning, check in at your resort, visit the bat sanctuary and Hagimit Falls in the afternoon, and enjoy a seafood barbecue dinner at the resort.
Time your early morning around the tide for Vanishing Island and snorkeling at Talikud Island, then head back to Davao after lunch.
A direct flight from Manila to Davao Airport (DVO) takes about
1 hour 50 minutes
, and about
1 hour 10 minutes
from Cebu. From the airport to Sasa wharf takes about
15–20 minutes
by taxi (about
) — the closest island-connecting wharf to the airport.
The most common route is crossing from Davao's Sasa wharf to Kinawitnon wharf in Samal's Babak area. A small passenger boat takes about
10–15 minutes
, at a fare of about
per person, while roll-on/roll-off boats that carry cars run almost around the
clock
. From Santa Ana wharf downtown, there are also passenger boats to Kaputian in southern Samal and to Talikud Island, taking about
30 minutes–1 hour
. Some upscale resorts, such as Pearl Farm Beach Resort, run their own private boats from Davao's Lanang area, so check the pickup arrangements when booking.
Tricycles, habal-habal (motorbike taxis), and multicabs wait in front of the wharf. To cover several sights, chartering a multicab for half a day to a full day (about
) or negotiating a route price with a habal-habal driver is convenient. If you've rented a car, you can also load it onto a roll-on/roll-off boat and drive freely around the island.
The Samal–Davao Connector Bridge (SIDC), a four-lane, toll-free bridge linking Davao's Lanang area to Samal Island, is under construction with a target completion of
. The timeline may slip further depending on funding, so check for the latest updates.
Like Davao, Samal Island sees little typhoon impact, and with year-round temperatures around 25–33 degrees, it's a beach destination in any season.
January
through
May
, with comparatively more clear days, is best, and
March–May
in particular has strong sunlight that brings out the most vivid sea colors. From
June
to
November
, afternoon showers are frequent, but they usually clear within an hour or two.
Vanishing Island's exposed hours shift with the tide, so check a tide table before visiting. On weekends, holidays, summer vacation (April–
May
), and Holy Week, Davao locals turn out in force, lengthening wharf waits and crowding popular resorts, so it's best to go on a weekday if possible. Timing your visit around Davao's
August
Kadayawan Festival is also a good way to combine a city festival with an island getaway.

Most accommodation on Samal Island is beach resorts. In the northwest Babak area closest to Davao, mid-range and water-park-style resorts cluster together, convenient for family travelers, at about
a night. The southern Kaputian side is quieter, with wider beaches, and upscale resorts like Pearl Farm Beach Resort run
and up a night. Budget cottages and guesthouses run about
but are fairly simple. The island doesn't have many restaurants or amenities, so it's best to choose a resort with meals included or bring snacks over from Davao.

Food centers on seafood barbecue. Resorts and beach restaurants let you pick fish, squid, and shrimp to be grilled over charcoal, and sea urchin and shellfish are also cheap in season. Kinilaw and grilled tuna jaw from tuna caught in Davao Gulf are also musts. Buying durian, marang, or mangosteen from a fruit stall in Davao to eat on the beach is another option, but check first, since most resorts prohibit bringing durian inside.
On weekend afternoons, the line for boats back to Davao gets long. Returning to the wharf before
4 p.m.
gives you a more comfortable crossing.
ATMs on the island are scarce and often out of order. Entrance fees, habal-habal, and bangka fares are often paid in cash, so it's best to bring enough from Davao.
It's best to negotiate the habal-habal fare, including destination and waiting time, before you board. For visiting several places, arranging a half-day contract with one driver is convenient.
The bat sanctuary has a strong smell. Bring a mask, and avoid flash photography, which startles the bats.
Many resorts limit day-pass numbers on weekends. It's safer to book popular resorts by the day before.
Snorkeling gear can be rented at resorts, but quality varies. If you snorkel often, it's worth bringing your own mask.
Phone signal is generally good across most areas but can be weak in the island's south and parts of Talikud.
Some beaches in Davao Gulf have plenty of sea urchins and sharp coral. Wear water shoes, and avoid stepping on or touching the coral.
The tide comes in quickly at Vanishing Island. Be sure to return to the boat by the time your bangka driver sets.
Ask for a life vest when boarding a small bangka, and avoid boats that carry more passengers than their limit.
Samal Island, like Davao City, has fairly strict rules on smoking and littering. Take your trash with you, and smoke only in designated areas.
Entering the cave or touching the bats is prohibited at the bat sanctuary. Contact with wildlife carries disease risks, so this rule must be followed.
Staying too long on a sandbar or in shallow water without knowing the tide schedule can leave you suddenly stranded. Be sure to agree on a return time with your bangka driver.
